analysis.one_liner: Tells the DOT to bar airlines from charging fees that exceed their actual costs.
analysis.headline: The FAIR Fees Act, introduced by two Senate Democrats, died in the Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote in the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Transportation to write rules banning airlines from charging fees—like change and cancellation fees and checked bag fees—that are unreasonable or way out of line with what the service actually costs the airline. It spelled out how regulators would judge whether a fee is fair: what it costs the airline to process a change or handle a bag, and whether the airline can easily resell the seat. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers who pay change and cancellation fees or checked bag fees. Airlines collected billions of dollars a year in these fees, and the bill would have let regulators cap them at roughly the airline's actual cost, potentially saving consumers hundreds of dollars per ticket change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Air travelers paying change and bag fees

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Transportation Department to prohibit air carriers from imposing fees that are unreasonable or disproportional to the costs the carrier actually incurs, and to set standards for making that judgment.
Covers three categories of fees: change or cancellation fees, checked bag fees, and any other fee an airline attaches to an interstate flight.

Requires regulators to weigh what a change or cancellation actually costs the airline—including processing costs, labor, and whether the freed-up seat gets resold—so fees would have to track real costs rather than serve as a profit center.
Requires the Department to update the standards at least every three years so the rules keep up with airline pricing practices.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would lose fee revenue that is currently pure margin—checked bag fees alone run into the billions of dollars annually. Some of that cost could be passed back to travelers through slightly higher base fares, though the fee itself would be limited to cost.

drawbacks.text: Airlines and free-market critics would argue the bill substitutes government cost accounting for market pricing, and that some of the lost fee revenue would simply be rolled into base fares, so flyers who never change plans or check bags could end up paying for those who do.

The standards are administratively demanding: regulators would have to estimate things like the resale value of a cancelled seat and the fare difference a replacement passenger pays, which invites disputes and litigation over every fee structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real and targeted: change fees of $200 on a seat the airline promptly resells are hard to defend as cost-proportional, and bag fees far exceed the marginal cost of handling luggage. The main honest cost is that airlines would likely reprice some of that revenue into base fares, and writing workable standards would take real regulatory effort. On balance, travelers as a group would likely come out ahead, with the gains concentrated among people who change plans or check bags.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on May 4, 2017, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the FAIR Fees Act on May 4, 2017, with Sen. Richard Blumenthal as the bill's sole cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action—no markup, no vote—and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off because the bill died: they kept the ability to charge change, cancellation, and bag fees with no requirement that the fees bear any relationship to their costs. Travelers who pay those fees are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which kept unregulated fee revenue

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Fees Act to require fee-cost proportionality rules for airlines.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut, sole cosponsor

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 4, 2017 and took no action—no markup, no vote—for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored the bill and no Republican ever signed on or voted on it, so the partisan shape of opposition was never recorded—the bill simply died in committee.

industries.note: Change and cancellation fees and checked bag fees are a multibillion-dollar revenue stream for the airline industry, largely above and beyond the cost of the service. The bill would have forced those fees down to roughly cost, which is why airline interests had every reason to prefer the bill stall in committee. Its interest in this bill ran against the travelers who pay the fees.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and fee-comparison services
industries.note: Airlines would have had to justify every fee against a regulator-set standard, making fee structures more standardized and easier for comparison tools to present. A smaller effect than the direct hit to airlines.
